A down payment can be one of the biggest hurdles to buying a home, NPR's Windsor Johnson reports
a new study finds saving enough can take years with wide differences across states.
A new study from Cinch Home Services estimates nearly three years nationally to save a 15%
down payment.
Hawaii has the longest wait, at about five years.
Iowa has the shortest, around a year and nine months.
Jess Fields, the company's chief commercial officer, says the national estimate assumes
that potential buyers are saving about $1,700 per month.
Let's just say if someone can only save $300 a month, it would take them about 15 years
to reach that down payment amount.
At $500 a month, it would still take over nine years to get to that goal.
And if home prices go up while buyers are saving, coming up with enough for a down payment
could take even longer.
Windsor Johnston, NPR News.
A historic drop for Google parent company Alphabet stock dragged the U.S. stock market lower
today.
This is NPR.
The Senate is unlikely to act on a House-passed bill that would make daylight saving time
permanent.
Supporters like President Trump argue that ending the time change would provide more
daylight during the times Americans are most active.
Opponents say commuters in some states wouldn't see the sun until after 9 a.m.
Daylight saving time ends early Sunday, requiring much of the U.S. to move clocks back one hour.
Walmart, Delta, Uber and DoorDash are among the companies facing an inquiry from federal
regulators about how they use consumers' personal data to set prices, NPR's Alina Seljuk reports.
The Federal Trade Commission has sent letters to nine companies, major retailers, airlines
and consumer apps.
The agency says it wants to look under the hood of how these firms charge different shoppers
and pay different gig workers for the same products or services.
For example, do people see different prices based on whether they're a member of a loyalty
program?
Or do delivery drivers get different wages based on how many orders they previously declined
to deliver?
The companies the FTC is ordering to answer its questions are Walmart, Target, Delta,
United, JetBlue, Uber, Lyft, DoorDash and Instacart.
Alina Seljuk, NPR News.

Sylvia Earle says there's no sustainable way to harvest krill without harming whales
